problem: The step calls 200 J the energy 'delivered to the patient' and then says the remainder is 'lost in paddles, cables and the chest wall'. Energy dissipated in the chest wall is already inside the energy delivered to the patient; it is not a separate loss. A student will be confused about which energy is stored, which is delivered, and which reaches the heart.
fix: Say: of the 400 J stored, part is lost in the internal resistance and cables of the defibrillator, so about 200–320 J is delivered to the chest. Of that delivered energy, only a fraction reaches the heart muscle, because most is dissipated in the chest wall. Internal defibrillation needs less stored energy for the same reason.

problem: The output stage is described only as delivering a pulse. The standard pacemaker output circuit has a coupling capacitor in series with the lead, so the pulse has zero net DC charge. Without it the electrode polarises and the heart does not respond; the point is missing.
fix: Add: the output stage has a series coupling capacitor. It blocks direct current, so each pulse is followed by a small opposite charge and the net charge injected into the tissue is zero. This prevents electrode polarisation and tissue damage.

problem: The arithmetic is right (2.0 Ah ÷ 0.0876 Ah per year = 22.8 years), but a student may take 22.8 years as a realistic implant life. Real pacemakers last roughly 5–12 years because of self-discharge, telemetry and higher current during pacing.
fix: Keep the answer 22.8 years as the calculated value, and add one line: this ideal figure ignores self-discharge and the higher current drawn during pacing and telemetry, so a real device lasts far less, typically under a decade.

problem: The text spells the cell as lithium-iodine but the figure writes only 'Li-I₂'. Readers with English as a second language may not connect the two names.
fix: Label the node: 'Lithium-iodine (Li-I₂) cell', note 'about 2.8 V'.
